items.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
items.abstract_or_text: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

items.title: The Reasoning Paradox in Scientific Sandboxes: Why Extended Reasoning Fails in Autonomous Bioinformatics and How to Fix It.
items.abstract_or_text: Frontier large language models (LLMs) trained with extended reasoning, such as DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI o1, have established state-of-the-art benchmarks in formal logic, competitive programming, and mathematics. In interactive, empirical scientific sandboxes, however, their efficacy remains counter-intuitive. In the Bioinformatics Benchmark (BixBench), extended reasoning models paradoxically degraded in multi-turn environments, leading benchmark authors to exclude them from primary agentic evaluations. In this paper, we conduct the first systematic forensic audit of the internal cognitive monologue ( ... ) of open-weight reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B) and matched instruction-tuned controls (Qwen2.5-Coder-14B) deployed inside containerized computational biology sandboxes on Nvidia H100 GPUs. Our forensic analysis uncovers two distinct systemic failure modes: (1) The PubMed Prior Trap, in which reasoning models engage in epistemic rationalization within their cognitive stream, falsely convincing themselves that empirical datasets are missing and substituting empirical computation with speculative literature recall (e.g., estimating adjusted p-values based on "typical experimental outcomes"); and (2) Tag Language Nesting Collisions, in which models conflate agent-level XML action tags with Python syntax, producing terminal interpreter syntax errors. To resolve this paradox, we introduce Dual Track Decoupled Reasoning (DTDR), an agent scaffolding architecture that evicts internal cognitive monologues from multi-turn history, injects strict empirical grounding guardrails, and dynamically intercepts runtime tool invocations. On a stratified diagnostic benchmark spanning single-cell RNA-seq, bulk differential expression (DESeq2), and genomic variant prioritization (n=22 per arm), DTDR rescues the 14B reasoning model from 0.0% to 9.09% accuracy (2/22), doubling the performance of the matched non-reasoning coder control (4.55%, 1/22) while slashing code execution errors by 81% (13.6% vs. 72.7%) and reducing average steps to solution by 66% (1.77 vs. 5.18 steps). All replication pipelines, prompts, and trajectory manifests are openly released.

items.title: Decoding Cell-type Specific Gene Regulation with CellReg3D by Integrating DNA Large Language Models and 3D Genome Structure
items.abstract_or_text: Gene regulation is a core biological mechanism crucial for organismal growth and development. Recent advances in deep learning, coupled with increasing computational resources, have enabled large-scale modelling of gene regulatory processes. While numerous models have been proposed, effectively capturing long-range genomic interactions remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce CellReg3D, a multiscale and multi-modal deep learning framework designed to model cell-type-specific gene regulation by integrating local sequence patterns with long-range genomic interactions. Existing approaches often overlook the contribution of 3D genome architecture and face limitations in combining sequence-based features with chromatin interaction data. Specifically, CellReg3D overcomes these gaps by leveraging a DNA language model to encode sequence-level information and incorporating Hi-C-derived 3D chromatin interactions to capture chromatin spatial organization. We demonstrate that CellReg3D effectively learns epigenetic patterns and chromatin activity states, achieving state-of-the-art performance in predicting epigenetic marks and gene expression profiles across multiple cell types. Using interpretable methods, we illustrate how the model identifies cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms and prioritizes functional non-coding variants. Furthermore, we apply CellReg3D to enhance the interpretation of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and uncover novel potential gene regulatory interactions. Overall, CellReg3D offers a integrative framework for decoding regulatory genomics, unifying sequence and 3D genome structure data to advance variant prioritization, disease mechanism discovery, and personalized functional genomics.

items.title: A Biologically Inspired Attention Model for Neural Signal Analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Understanding how the brain represents sensory information and triggers behavioural responses is a fundamental goal in neuroscience. Recent advances in neuronal recording techniques aim to progress towards this milestone, yet the resulting high-dimensional responses are challenging to interpret and link to relevant variables. Although existing machine learning models propose to do so, they often sacrifice interpretability for predictive power, effectively operating as black boxes. In this work, we introduce SPARKS, a biologically inspired model capable of high decoding accuracy and interpretable discovery within a single framework. SPARKS adapts the self-attention mechanism of large language models to extract information from the timing of single spikes and the sequence in which neurons fire using Hebbian learning. Trained with a criterion inspired by predictive coding to enforce temporal coherence, our model produces low-dimensional latent embeddings that are robust across sessions and animals. By directly capturing the underlying data distribution through a generative encoding-decoding framework, SPARKS matches or exceeds state-of-the-art decoders across diverse electrophysiology and calcium imaging datasets from the motor, visual and entorhinal cortices. Crucially, the Hebbian coefficients learned by the model are interpretable, allowing us to infer directed functional interactions and recover the known functional hierarchy of the mouse visual cortex. Overall, SPARKS unifies representation learning, high-performance decoding and model interpretability in a single framework by bridging neuroscience and AI, providing a powerful and versatile tool for dissecting neural computations and marking a step towards the next generation of biologically inspired intelligent systems.

items.title: Silent methodological failures in AI-assisted science: benchmarking large language model agents for virtual gene knockout analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in computational biology, yet their reliability in executing complex scientific workflows remains poorly characterized. Here, we benchmarked five LLM agents (DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM 5.1, HY3 Preview, Kimi K2.6, and Minimax M2.7) on virtual gene knockout analyses using four computational frameworks across two single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets. All agents successfully completed the assigned workflows, but their quantitative outputs varied substantially: execution times spanned a 31fold range (61 − 1,920 s), while cross-model coefficients of variation reached 142.1%. Notably, four of five agents (80%) exhibited “silent methodological failures,” generating computationally valid, error-free code that produced biologically implausible results. Among the evaluated agents, GLM 5.1 showed the most balanced performance across computational efficiency and biological plausibility. These findings demonstrate that successful code execution alone does not ensure scientific validity and highlight cross-model concordance and biological validation as important quality-control strategies for Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted computational biology workflows.

items.title: SMILE: A Structured Multi-Agent Clinical Reasoning for Liver Ultrasound Understanding
items.abstract_or_text: Automated liver ultrasound report generation improves the diagnosis of liver diseases by producing clinically structured descriptions of anatomical and disease-related findings. However, current generative vision-language models (VLMs) often rely on a single reasoning pathway that maps ultrasound appearance directly to textual descriptions. In addition to the inherent vision-language modality gap, this design is limited for liver ultrasound because disease interpretation is constrained by subtle visual evidence, heterogeneous disease patterns, and limited paired supervision. To address these limitations, we propose SMILE, a Structured Multi-agent clInicaL rEasoning framework that uses multiple complementary specialist agents to interpret ultrasound images and consolidates their outputs through a judge-guided consensus mechanism. Our approach employs three specialized agents: an image interpretation agent for morphological descriptions, a clinical-stage reasoning agent, and a visual question answering (VQA) agent for targeted queries. These agent responses are then aggregated and scrutinized by a judge VLM using a consensus filtering prompt to produce a unified, clinically coherent output. Across a public liver ultrasound dataset and an internal clinical dataset, SMILE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art VLMs, achieving up to 19.0\% improvement in ROUGE-1 and 18.8\% improvement in clinical F1-score, while reaching VQA F1-scores of 0.82 and 0.65 on public and internal datasets, respectively. These results demonstrate the potential of SMILE for data-scarce and limited-supervision clinical settings. Our models, datasets, and code are available https://github.com/CMME-Lab/SMILE{here}.

items.title: Integrated Multi-Omics and Machine Learning Identify PTTG1 as a Prognostic Biomarker and Therapeutic Target in Endometrial Cancer
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) exhibits high molecular heterogeneity, and the lack of precise prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets severely limits the clinical management of high-risk patients. This study aimed to identify a robust multi-omics biomarker and elucidate its intrinsic oncogenic mechanisms and extrinsic immune-remodeling roles in the UCEC microenvironment. Methods We systematically integrated transcriptomic data from TCGA and GEO cohorts. WGCNA coupled with four machine learning algorithms (LASSO, SVM-RFE, XGBoost, Boruta) were employed for feature selection. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were integrated to map the cellular landscape. In silico virtual knockout, virtual overexpression, and pharmacogenomic analyses were conducted. Computational predictions were experimentally validated using Western blot, qRT-PCR, and immunohistochemistry in paired clinical specimens, and corroborated by CPTAC proteomic analysis. Results PTTG1 was identified as an independent prognostic biomarker, with significant overexpression confirmed at both mRNA and protein levels and predominant nuclear localization in tumor epithelium. Mechanistically, virtual knockout revealed PTTG1 drives malignant progression through hyperactivation of cell cycle, ribosome biogenesis, and glutathione metabolism, whereas virtual overexpression activated immune-related transcriptional networks including MHC class II antigen presentation. Integrated scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics demonstrated PTTG1 enrichment in malignant epithelial cells and tumor-associated macrophages. Drug sensitivity predictions identified selective vulnerability to MEK inhibitors, including selumetinib and trametinib. Conclusion PTTG1 serves as a multidimensional oncogenic driver and independent prognostic biomarker in UCEC, intrinsically fueling tumor proliferation while extrinsically orchestrating an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Bidirectional in silico perturbation revealed distinct transcriptional consequences, substantiated by multi-level experimental validation. Drug sensitivity predictions identified selective MEK inhibitor vulnerabilities, providing a rationale for PTTG1-guided prognostic stratification and targeted therapeutic strategies in high-risk UCEC.

items.title: Few-shot regulatory sequence design with a genomic language model
items.abstract_or_text: A central challenge in generative biology is translating knowledge learned from natural sequences and experiments into designs with desired functions. In-context learning (ICL) is an emergent capability of large language models that allows them to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without additional training, enabling these models to become general-purpose learners. Here, we show that the genome language model, Evo 2, exhibits generative ICL in biological sequence design. Prompting with just tens of examples conditions Evo 2 to generate novel and diverse regulatory DNA sequences without any additional training. Mechanistic analysis suggests that genomic ICL may originate from induction, similar to phenomena observed in natural language. Reinforcement learning leveraging sequence-to-function models as experiment-derived rewards further strengthens ICL. We first validate this approach by generating enhancers that drive cell-type-specific gene expression in three human cell lines. Extending this approach in vivo, enhancers designed using human regulatory element data selectively label layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the mouse cortex with high specificity and stronger activity than existing enhancers. Our study provides evidence of emergent properties in genomic sequence models and introduces a promising approach for improving functional conditioning in generative biology.

items.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Links Group-Specific Plasma Proteomics to Regional Structural Neuroimaging in Alzheimer's Disease
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology begins years before clinical symptoms, highlighting the need for scalable biomarkers that capture biological changes across the AD continuum. Broader plasma proteomics may capture systemic processes that vary with disease stage, yet their relationship to AD-related brain neurodegeneration remains unclear. We aimed to identify plasma proteomic signatures across cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD and evaluate their neuroanatomical associations. Methods: We analyzed 146 plasma analytes from 565 Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants (58 CN, 396 MCI, 111 AD). Group-specific proteomic signatures were identified using pairwise classification models with nested 5*5 cross-validation. SHAP quantified feature importance, with the top 15 proteins per comparison being prioritized for MRI association analysis. We analyzed 103 regional structural MRI volumes harmonized across 57 acquisition sites using ComBat. Separate ordinary least squares regression tested protein-MRI associations, adjusting for age, sex, APOE4, diagnosis, and intracranial volume, followed by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Results: Classification models using proteomic data achieved AUC of 0.956 +- 0.017 for CN vs MCI, 0.963 +- 0.011 for MCI vs. AD, and 0.836 +- 0.085 for CN vs. AD. SHAP identified group-dependent proteomic signatures. No protein-MRI associations survived FDR correction for CN vs. MCI. In MCI vs. AD, higher cortisol was associated with lower left precuneus and superior parietal volumes, while higher osteopontin was associated with lower left paracentral and accumbens volumes. In CN vs. AD, higher vitronectin was associated with lower posterior corpus callosum volume. Conclusion: These findings suggest that plasma proteomics capture group-specific systemic biological signals across the AD continuum. Linking ML-prioritized plasma proteins to regional brain structure provides neuroanatomical context for blood-based biomarker discovery.

items.title: CloneVI: A deep generative model for deciphering the relationships between cell state and mitochondrial genotype
items.abstract_or_text: Cellular diversity arises from both genetic lineages and non-genetic regulation of cell states, and knowing which cell states are tied to lineages is central to understanding how clones shape disease. Single-cell multi-omics technologies measure mitochondrial DNA mutations together with gene expression or chromatin accessibility in the same cells, but clones are usually inferred from mutations alone, making such clones difficult to identify. We developed CloneVI, a deep generative model that infers clonal structure from a latent cell state derived from gene expression or chromatin accessibility. It estimates the clonal probability of each cell from this cell state, together with the allele frequency of each clone by reconstructing the observed mutation counts. In simulated data, CloneVI recovered the ground-truth clonal structure in both single-clone and mixed-clone cell populations. In clonal hematopoiesis single-cell RNA-seq data with enriched mitochondrial transcripts, the inferred clones were associated with specific mitochondrial DNA mutations, and some of them showed high expression of a T-cell receptor variable-region gene. In chronic lymphocytic leukemia mitochondrial single-cell ATAC-seq data, CloneVI separated populations with different heteroplasmy levels and identified increased PAX9 accessibility. In a multi-donor ovarian tumor cohort, CloneVI captured mutant-cell populations enriched in particular cell states, and a differential test weighted by the clonal probability revealed the transcription factor activity of the cell state in which the mutant cells concentrated. CloneVI thus identifies populations defined by mitochondrial DNA mutations and associated with cell states in single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data. CloneVI is available at https://github.com/TaichiHIBI/cloneVI.

items.title: Current gaps in downstream applications of fMRI foundation models: lessons learned from BrainLM & BrainHarmonix on Prevent-AD
items.abstract_or_text: Foundation models have driven major advancements in the language and vision domains, as seen in the popularity of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, and a growing number of studies are bringing the approach to human brain imaging. Whether these models are ready for independent researchers to use on clinical datasets has yet to be examined. We evaluated two recent fMRI foundation models, BrainLM and BrainHarmonix, on PreventAD, a dataset on adults with a family history of Alzheimers disease. We compared features from frozen and fine-tuned models against two baselines: functional connectivity and a dummy classifier that always predicts the most common class. The sample includes 343 subjects who passed quality control, with a subset of 218 who had amyloid PET imaging. We tested four prediction targets: sex, age, progression to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and {beta}-amyloid burden. Both models required substantial changes to the released code. BrainLMs own data preparation workflow did not produce stable fine-tuning, which we achieved only after switching to a standard workflow implemented with the library Nilearn. BrainHarmonixs documentation did not specify how to normalize new data, so we resolved this by testing different alternatives. For sex, functional connectivity outperformed all foundation model features. For age group, the best foundation model feature, taken from BrainHarmonixs structural (T1-weighted) encoder, slightly exceeded functional connectivity, but the difference was not significant. For MCI and {beta}-amyloid, no feature exceeded the dummy classifier in accuracy, and the area under the curve (AUC) stayed near chance for all features. For both clinical targets, the most precise feature came from fine-tuned BrainLM, meaning a larger share of its positive predictions were correct than for functional connectivity, but neither difference reached statistical significance. These results suggested that the strong transfer to new tasks seen in large language models cannot yet be assumed for fMRI foundation models, and that both models required code adaptation that would preclude their streamlined adoption by independent groups. We recommend that future studies provide standardized data workflows and always report functional connectivity and dummy classifier baselines. For clinical targets with strong class imbalance, studies should report several metrics, including precision.

items.title: A Scoping Review of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Spatio-temporal Infectious Disease Forecasting
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Infectious diseases spread across space and time, yet most artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models treat forecasting as a purely temporal problem. We conducted a scoping review of AI/ML methods for spatio-temporal infectious disease forecasting, searching five databases on 20th November 2025. We included 93 studies published between 2018 and 2026, spanning 14 infectious diseases. Recurrent neural networks (46%) and graph neural networks (39%) dominated, with hybrid mechanistic-ML models growing steadily after 2022. Over 30 distinct error metrics were used, with no shared benchmarks, making cross-study comparison infeasible. Uncertainty was quantified in only 19% of studies, external validation in 13%, and 71% did not share code openly. Forecasts were concentrated in middle- and high-income countries, and only one study conducted fairness analysis. Addressing these gaps in evaluation standardisation, transparency, and equity is essential for AI/ML forecasting to inform public health policy.

items.title: Single-cell transcriptomics of enriched rare neural lineages of Tribolium castaneum
items.abstract_or_text: Background Single-cell transcriptomic atlases have transformed our understanding of cell diversity. However, studies designed to profile entire tissues or organisms often omit or underrepresent rare cell populations. Enriching selected populations before sequencing offers a powerful approach to overcoming this limitation, but its application in insects has largely focused on Drosophila, limiting opportunities for comparative studies. Here, we establish complementary workflows for targeted transcriptomic profiling of rare neural populations in the red flour beetle, Tribolium castaneum. Results We developed two workflows combining population enrichment with single-cell or single-nucleus RNA sequencing. First, we generated cell suspensions from a transgenic reporter line labelling embryonic neuroblasts, enriched fluorescently labelled cells by fluorescence-activated cell sorting, and performed single-cell RNA sequencing. Second, we immunolabelled first-instar larval brains with an antibody against the nuclear transcription factor Rx, isolated and sorted labelled nuclei, and performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Both workflows yielded material suitable for transcriptomic profiling, demonstrating complementary reporter-based and antibody-based strategies for accessing selected neural populations at different developmental stages. Conclusions These workflows establish a methodological framework for targeted single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomic studies of rare or specific neural populations in Tribolium. They provide practical starting points for adaptation to other insect systems, expanding opportunities for comparative investigations of neural development and cell-type evolution.

items.title: Integrative Transcriptomic Meta-Analysis Reveals SIRT1-SNCA Correlation in Parkinson's Disease
items.abstract_or_text: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects midbrain dopaminergic neurons without any approved therapy. Candidate molecular targets identified in one model are not always traceable across the postmortem, induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC), and cell-based systems used to study PD, which complicates clinical translation. To address this gap, we performed an integrative transcriptomic meta-analysis of 33 publicly available datasets across postmortem human brain, iPSC-derived models, and dopaminergic cell lines of PD. Differential expression and functional enrichment analyses were combined with STRING protein-protein interaction networks, followed by drug-gene interaction screening against a polyphenol panel. Overall, resveratrol was recovered in all 33 comparisons, independent of model system, tissue, and genetic background. We associated resveratrol with 30 distinct target genes, and SIRT1 was itself a recovered target in 6 comparisons spanning all three model systems. Finally, we resolved the SIRT1-SNCA relationship into four directional patterns that differed by model, inverse in postmortem brain and positive in acutely toxin-exposed cells. These findings support a candidate, context-dependent resveratrol-SIRT1 axis in PD.

items.title: Spectral Adaptive Repositioning for Flow-Based Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling
items.abstract_or_text: Predicting transcriptome-wide cellular responses to genetic and biomolecular perturbations is central to functional genomics and therapeutic target discovery. Existing methods assign gene positional encodings derived from arbitrary orderings or static co-expression masks built from unperturbed cells, and cannot capture the functional rewiring induced by perturbations. We present SPEAR, a generative framework built on two complementary positional mechanisms. Spectral positional encoding grounds each gene's position in the geometry of the co-expression network via continuous coordinates derived from the graph Laplacian. Adaptive repositioning then derives each gene's position from its perturbation-conditioned hidden state at every layer, allowing the attention genes exert on one another to reorganize without explicit supervision. Evaluated on genetic, pharmacological, and cytokine perturbation benchmarks, SPEAR demonstrates excellent recovery of differential gene-expression, distributional structure, and perturbation-specific identifiability. SPEAR also captures latent positional relationships that closely map to known transcription factor-target interactions. https://github.com/shouryaverma/SPEAR}{https://github.com/shouryaverma/SPEAR

items.title: PaleoRigor: a bounded research agent with a reproducible evidence trail for paleomicrobiome data processing
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Ancient microbial evidence informs research on past health, diet, and environments, but its scarcity and susceptibility to contamination demand care in selecting and processing data. Language models can now turn a research request into an analysis plan, but an unconstrained planner may reference files that do not exist, apply operations a format forbids, or answer a question the data cannot settle. A planner used on such evidence therefore needs to be bounded, and its decisions recoverable afterwards. Results: We developed PaleoRigor around three commitments. Agent: a language model plans the analysis. Constraint: a validator checks every file reference, format and step dependency before anything runs, execution is restricted to predefined local modules, and a planning contract directs the model to refuse out-of-scope requests with a named reason code rather than answer them. Reproducibility: each run is exported with its plan, intermediate files, checksums and decisions. In a preregistered, frozen held-out evaluation, PaleoRigor passed 23 of 24 runs (95.8%; Wilson 95% confidence interval, 79.8-99.3%): 11 of 12 supported runs and all 12 prespecified boundary decisions. An ablation that removed this planning contract from the same model passed 19 of 24 (79.2%). Repeating the frozen design with a second model configuration yielded 24 of 24 successes for PaleoRigor and 19 of 24 for the ablated arm. Pooled post hoc across both configurations, PaleoRigor passed 47 of 48 runs (97.9%), compared with 38 of 48 (79.2%) for the ablated arms. All 96 run labels were recomputed from retained records and matched. Dataset-level tests matched read counts and compressed-file sizes for six public sequencing records and documented the removal of 114 duplicate sequence entries. A retraction-associated audit illustrated how expert review limited conclusions to file-level evidence. Conclusions: For paleomicrobiome data, pairing a language-model agent with explicit constraints and a reproducible record makes the agent's proposed analysis reviewable before its outputs support a biological claim. PaleoRigor delivers checked inputs, a recorded transformation history and a named reason for each request it refuses, and runs as a local desktop application. It prepares data for specialist analysis; ancient-DNA authentication and biological interpretation remain with the paleobiologist.

items.title: MIMIC-Note-Extract: A Large-Scale Structured Dataset Extracted from MIMIC-IV-Note Discharge Summaries
items.abstract_or_text: MIMIC is one of the most widely used public hospital datasets for machine learning on electronic health records, yet clinically important information, such as past medical history, allergies, and diagnostic findings, remains confined to free-text discharge summaries. Studies requiring this information must therefore build their own extraction pipelines, duplicating substantial effort across projects. We release MIMIC-Note-Extract (MNE), a large-scale dataset that uses a hybrid extraction pipeline combining deterministic parsing with schema-guided large language model generation to transform 16 sections from 300,720 discharge summaries into structured tables. MNE adds information that has no structured MIMIC counterpart and enriches related tables with broader coverage and greater clinical detail, including 10 times more patient-history entries and medication histories for more than twice as many admissions. Validation by medical doctors confirms extraction accuracy above 92% across sections. Using MNE, we construct a clinical decision-making benchmark for LLM agents, demonstrating how reusable structured representations of clinical narratives reduce data curation effort.

items.title: LabWeaver: reliable agentic data analysis grounded in laboratory knowled
items.abstract_or_text: Agentic systems powered by large language models are rapidly automating biological data analysis. However, their reliability remains questionable because they often overlook experimental context, such as disease domain and experimental protocol. Existing agentic systems organize context around individual users and projects, whereas research is organized around laboratories whose projects share experimental context. As a result, experimental context learned in one project remains unavailable to related projects. We introduce LabWeaver, an agentic data analysis framework with a laboratory-organized architecture of three tiers: laboratory, user and project. Further, LabWeaver distills experimental context into laboratory memory and skills, which are shared across users and projects after human-gated review. To isolate the contribution of experimental context, we analyzed a synovial sarcoma single-cell RNA-seq dataset in two sessions that differed only in whether laboratory memory and skills were available. The context-free session lost the fusion reporter at read alignment and misannotated the tumor cells. In contrast, the context-enabled session recovered reporter expression and resolved five fusion-anchored tumor cell states.

items.title: Integrated Biomarker Profiling Uncovers a Distinct Pathophysiological Signature of Long COVID
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Long COVID, a post-infectious syndrome is caracterized by multitude interconnected pathophysiological mechanisms involving both genetic and environmental factors. Due to these complications, diagnosis remains an area of ongoing research because of the lack of reliable and robust biological markers. The development of biomarkers that reflect the biological mechanism(s) involved in the disease will enable accurate diagnosis, prevent misdiagnosis and, above all, facilitate the proper design of therapeutic trials based on these biomarkers and their modulation. We performed a multi-omics analysis of plasma samples from 222 participants: 100 well-characterised long-COVID patients (LC), 62 individuals with resolved-COVID (RC), and 60 uninfected controls (UC). We integrated state-of-the-art nuclear magnetic resonance metabolomics and lipoproteomics with multiplexed assays screening immune, vascular, and mitochondrial stress markers. LC patients exhibited a distinct signature of persistent thrombo-inflammation and bioenergetic alteration. We identified a systemic metabolic rewiring characterised by depleted pyruvate and lactate levels, indicating impaired glycolytic throughput, with evidence of altered alternative compensatory glutamine-dependent and enhanced ketone body-driven anapleurosis. The immunovascular profile revealed chronic platelet and neutrophil activation, as well as high levels of angiogenesis and matrix metalloproteinases, suggesting vascular damage. Furthermore, LC patients demonstrated a pro-atherogenic lipoproteomic profile. A XGBoost machine learning model integrating these markers could identify LC patients with 100% accuracy. Our results show that LC is defined by a breakdown in energy metabolism and microvascular integrity. The identification of accurate multi-omics signature provides a robust framework for objective clinical diagnosis and paves the way for targeted therapies to improve patient care and advance precision medicine.

items.title: CTLA-4 checkpoint signalling modulates germinal centre dynamics and antibody avidity during Borrelia burgdorferi infection in mice.
items.abstract_or_text: Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative agent of Lyme borreliosis, persists in mammalian hosts despite robust activation of innate and adaptive immunity. A hallmark of murine infection is the production of low-avidity antibodies, yet the immunological mechanisms underlying this defective humoral response remain poorly understood. Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing of draining lymph node cells from Borrelia-infected mice at days 7 and 14 post-infection, comparing transcriptional profiles with those from mice immunised with heat-killed Borrelia or with a potent germinal centre-inducing protein immunisation. Borrelia infection induced a rapid germinal centre response, however, light zone B cells displayed diminished expression of co-stimulatory and T-B cell interaction molecules while maintaining core germinal centre identity markers, suggesting impaired positive selection. T follicular helper cells upregulated multiple inhibitory checkpoint receptor genes, most prominently Ctla4, alongside an active germinal centre engagement programme. Foxp3? regulatory T cells upregulated genes associated with follicular-homing and suppressive function, including those implicated in CTLA-4-mediated trans-endocytosis. To test whether inhibitory signalling contributes to the impaired humoral response, infected mice were treated with anti-CTLA-4 blocking antibody. CTLA-4 blockade significantly increased plasma cell numbers and enhanced both the magnitude and avidity of Borrelia-specific IgG responses, including the induction of complement-fixing IgG2a. These findings reveal that CTLA-4-dependent inhibitory signalling contributes to defective antibody quality during Borrelia infection, identifying a mechanism by which dysregulated T cell responses may facilitate impaired humoral control of a persistent spirochaetal pathogen.

items.title: Beyond Diagnosis: A Scoping Review of Machine Learning and NLP for Multilevel Mental Health Factors in Population Crises
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Natural disasters, pandemics, armed conflict, and economic upheaval inflict lasting harm on mental wellbeing, yet what determines who recovers and who deteriorates remains poorly understood across crisis types. Objectives: This review maps how crisis exposure shapes wellbeing across four crisis typologies, two surveillance modes (NLP-based and survey/administrative), and three impact directions (favorable, adverse, or mixed).Eligibility criteria: Peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers published in English between 2016 and 2026, applying machine learning, NLP, or deep learning methods to a population exposed to one of the four crisis typologies, and reporting at least one measurable mental health outcome.Sources of evidence: PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore, supplemented by forward and backward citation searching and targeted keyword searches.Charting methods: Factors were charted using the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health framework, adapted for the health system where the framework’s coverage is thinnest. They were sorted into tiers, subgroups, and subdimensions with maximum possible fidelity to the original framework. Results: Across 338 codeable determinants, Intermediary Determinants, particularly psychosocial and behavioral-biological factors, accounted for two-thirds of coded determinants, while NLP-based methods proved most effective at capturing structural and contextual signals (e.g., governance, discourse-based constructs) rather than the clinical burden measures that dominate closer to the individual. Favorable, protective constructs were both rarer and less computationally detected than adverse ones, concentrating almost entirely in mastery, self-concept, coping, and social capital. Forty-five factors were set aside as Outcome Measures because they described prior symptoms, diagnoses, or the study's own outcome construct, with 8 being circular with the study's stated target. Fewer studies examined economic downturns, and conflict studies had almost no NLP presence. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate this field has matured methodologically in adverse detection but remains structurally limited in reach. This is most evident in armed conflict contexts and in the surveillance of protective, resilience-oriented signals, highlighting the need for digital phenotyping, expanded NLP coverage, and wider adoption of explainable AI methods.

items.title: Beyond Diagnosis: A Scoping Review of Machine Learning and NLP for Multilevel Mental Health Factors in Population Crises
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Natural disasters, pandemics, armed conflict, and economic upheaval inflict lasting harm on mental wellbeing, yet what determines who recovers and who deteriorates remains poorly understood across crisis types. Objectives: This review maps how crisis exposure shapes wellbeing across four crisis typologies, two surveillance modes (NLP-based and survey/administrative), and three impact directions (favorable, adverse, or mixed).Eligibility criteria: Peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers published in English between 2016 and 2026, applying machine learning, NLP, or deep learning methods to a population exposed to one of the four crisis typologies, and reporting at least one measurable mental health outcome.Sources of evidence: PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore, supplemented by forward and backward citation searching and targeted keyword searches.Charting methods: Factors were charted using the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health framework, adapted for the health system where the framework’s coverage is thinnest. They were sorted into tiers, subgroups, and subdimensions with maximum possible fidelity to the original framework. Results: Across 338 codeable determinants, Intermediary Determinants, particularly psychosocial and behavioral-biological factors, accounted for two-thirds of coded determinants, while NLP-based methods proved most effective at capturing structural and contextual signals (e.g., governance, discourse-based constructs) rather than the clinical burden measures that dominate closer to the individual. Favorable, protective constructs were both rarer and less computationally detected than adverse ones, concentrating almost entirely in mastery, self-concept, coping, and social capital. Forty-five factors were set aside as Outcome Measures because they described prior symptoms, diagnoses, or the study's own outcome construct, with 8 being circular with the study's stated target. Fewer studies examined economic downturns, and conflict studies had almost no NLP presence. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate this field has matured methodologically in adverse detection but remains structurally limited in reach. This is most evident in armed conflict contexts and in the surveillance of protective, resilience-oriented signals, highlighting the need for digital phenotyping, expanded NLP coverage, and wider adoption of explainable AI methods.

items.title: Conserved synaptic modifications by humanized tau through diverse isoform- and mutation-specific intracellular interactions
items.abstract_or_text: Mutations in the microtubule-binding protein tau are considered causal for a diverse group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively referred to as primary tauopathies. Specific tauopathies are associated with different mutations, distinct tau isoforms, manifest in unique cellular and circuit-wide patterns of degeneration, and present with specific clinical symptoms and trajectories. The mechanisms that link variations in the primary tau protein structure to distinct forms of neural circuit dysfunction remain largely unknown. Here, we created an orthogonal viral resource to systematically examine the impact of expressing humanized tau isoforms harboring different disease-relevant mutations in excitatory pyramidal cells from the mouse prelimbic cortex. We used these reagents to show that expression of mutant humanized tau (hTau) as either of two isoforms produced very similar patterns of circuit-specific synaptic disconnection on cortical projection neurons. However, mass spectrometry revealed that the interactomes of these different tau species varied markedly as functions of isoform, mutation, and subcellular location. We validated the functional relevance of increased hTau interactions with mitochondrial proteins in induced neurons differentiated from Ngn2-iPSCs expressing different hTau constructs. These results suggest different disease-relevant hTau proteins likely use distinct mechanisms to drive a highly stereotyped form of synapse loss in cortical neurons.

items.title: GPBench: A benchmark framework for genomic prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Genomic prediction (GP) has emerged as a powerful data mining strategy for disease risk assessment and molecular breeding. GP leverages genome-wide genetic variations and phenotypic information through a computational model to estimate genetic potential or disease risk. However, the field of GP still faces several major challenges: (i) dataset bias and insufficient representativeness; (ii) the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and a systematic benchmarking framework; (iii) heavy reliance on empirical expertise for experimental result interpretation, which hinders large-scale and systematic analysis. These issues make it difficult to conduct systematic cross-species evaluation and comparison of GP methods, and their authentic applications. To address these challenges, we established a standardized and extensible GP benchmark framework-GPBench. We first collected and harmonized public datasets from 16 species, covering animals, plants, and microorganisms, comprising 57 traits, 40,821 samples, and 493,821 single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Then, using the standardized datasets, the framework evaluates 21 GP models and provides a unified assessment across four dimensions: effectiveness, sensitivity, robustness, and scalability. Furthermore, we developed a large language model-based intelligent analysis system to facilitate the interpretation of GP experiments and model recommendations. GPBench provides the community with a fair, unified, and scalable platform (https://www.sdu-idea.cn/GPBench/) and an open-source library for comparing and optimizing GP methods, ultimately accelerating the application of GP in life sciences and biomedical research.

items.title: Disentangling Context-Specific Alzheimer's Disease Progression Signatures through an Explainable AI Framework
items.abstract_or_text: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression involves stage-dependent transcriptional changes that are often masked by dominant cellular and biological variation. Here, we present ADVISE (Alzheimer's Disease Variational Isolation of Signal Embeddings), an interpretable deep generative framework designed to disentangle Braak stage-associated transcriptional signals from background biological variation through separate latent representations. Using explainable AI, ADVISE prioritizes genes and pathways contributing to the disease-specific representation. Applying ADVISE to large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from the human prefrontal cortex, we identify shared and context-specific signatures of AD progression across global, sex-specific, and cell-type-specific analyses, revealing convergent molecular programs involving synaptic transmission, HSF1-associated proteostatic stress responses, and SLIT/ROBO axon guidance. Notably, ADVISE prioritizes ROBO2 as a progression-associated candidate in excitatory neurons. Experimental validation using CRISPR activation in hiPSC-derived excitatory neurons demonstrates that ROBO2 activation reduces the phosphorylated Tau-to-total Tau ratio. ADVISE thus reveals context-dependent molecular signatures of AD progression and bridges human single-cell discoveries with experimental validation of candidate regulators of AD pathology.

items.title: Omics-scale decoding of protein N-glycosylation using protein language model embeddings
items.abstract_or_text: Protein language models (pLMs) learn rich sequence semantics from vast volume of protein sequences, yet the information encoded in their high-dimensional embeddings remains largely a black box, posing an interpretability challenge. Here we show that semantic features learned by pLMs can be decoded to reveal biologically meaningful signals using coevolutionary analysis without downstream supervised-training. Building on this insight, we developed MaskNGly, a zero-shot framework that identifies protein N-glycosylation sites directly from PLM-embeddings while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised predictors. MaskNGly is computationally efficient and intrinsically transferable, enabling omics-scale characterization of protein glycosylation landscape. Applied across proteomes, it reveals that canonical N-X-S/T motifs gain higher glycosylation propensities with increasing organismal complexity and that glycosylation preferentially occurs at structured, solvent-exposed regions. Mutations altering high-scoring motifs are more frequently disease-associated. The framework also captures signatures of glycosylation-mediated protein allostery. These results establish an interpretable and scalable route to study glycobiology from pLM-embeddings.

items.title: Where single-cell foundation models help: a benchmark of annotation, perturbation and regulatory inference against simple baselines
items.abstract_or_text: Single-cell foundation models (FMs) are proposed as general tools for cell-type annotation, in silico perturbation and gene-regulatory-network (GRN) inference. To identify where they add value, we benchmarked five FMs (scGPT, Geneformer V1 and V2, Nicheformer, scFoundation), CellOracle, supervised perturbation models including STATE, and task-matched simple baselines on the same data, from K562 Perturb-seq screens and primary cells to healthy-donor and isogenic leukodystrophy brain organoids, a public organoid CRISPR screen and lung cancer biopsies. FMs were most useful when labels had to be transferred across species: from human to mouse lung, Nicheformer reached 0.98 accuracy and Geneformer V2 and scFoundation about 0.90, against 0.68 for the best baseline. Zero-shot in silico perturbations captured the direction of real responses in K562, with up to 75% of perturbations shifted in the expected direction (scFoundation, p < 1e-8), and Geneformer V2 networks recovered patient-level tumour differential expression better than co-expression (fold enrichment 2.9 versus 2.0). Within a species, FM embeddings annotated cells as accurately as principal components. In organoids, predicted knockout effects were largely explained by where the target is expressed, and an expression-matched control test isolated the gene-specific part, 12 to 35% of the effects. Isogenic Canavan and Krabbe organoids and 4H patient organoids, with one library per line and time point, did not yet separate methods from differences between clones and donors, which defines the replication needed for future validation. Fine-tuning changed classification accuracy but not knockout rankings. We release the benchmark, baselines, pipeline checks and the isogenic reference task as the fmaudit package, so that new models can be evaluated on the tasks where FMs already help.

items.title: A candidate HNRNPU-CHD2 RNA-processing axis in neurodevelopmental disease
items.abstract_or_text: Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in HNRNPU, which encodes a nuclear RNA-binding scaffold protein, cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy, intellectual disability and brain malformations, but the programs that link HNRNPU dosage to neuronal dysfunction remain poorly defined. We depleted HNRNPU in Human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK293T) cells, profiled gene expression and alternative splicing, intersected the two datasets, and asked which of the resulting genes already carried a neurodevelopmental annotation. Knockdown produced 5,643 differentially expressed genes and 21,728 high-confidence splicing events; 1,222 genes changed at both levels, and two pre-specified neurodevelopmental panel genes were among them: CHD2 and DYRK1A. In K562 eCLIP experiments, 107 reproducible HNRNPU peaks were detected across the CHD2 gene body, and three of the four regulated exons introduce a reading-frame shift whose premature termination codon lies far upstream of the final exon junction, predicting nonsense-mediated decay. Public K562 knockdown data reproduced the rise in CHD2 mRNA and the same skipped-exon change, and CHD2 depletion in the neural line SH-SY5Y altered cell-cycle, DNA-repair and neural gene programs. HNRNPU therefore constrains a frameshift-prone splicing switch in CHD2, a candidate route from HNRNPU haploinsufficiency to loss of functional CHD2 if these transcripts are degraded.

items.title: Integrative Pan-Cancer Multi-Omics Analysis Reveals POLQ as a Prognostic Biomarker and Immunotherapeutic Target in Uterine Corpus Endometrial Carcinoma
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract DNA polymerase theta (POLQ) mediates microhomology-mediated end joining and represents a synthetic lethal target for homologous recombination deficient cancers, yet its pan-cancer clinical, immunoregulatory and predictive functions are poorly defined. Multi-omics data from TCGA, GTEx, cBioPortal, TIMER2.0 and GSCA were used for pan-cancer profiling of POLQ expression, mutations, prognosis, immune signatures. Drug sensitivity correlation analysis together with in silico molecular docking simulations were applied to predict potential binding between POLQ and candidate therapeutic agents. Differential gene expression analysis and functional enrichment were further investigated in uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC). POLQ was overexpressed in most malignancies, associated with advanced stages and poor survival. Gene amplification drove its upregulation. POLQ expression showed significant correlations with immune cell infiltration, tumor mutation burden, and microsatellite instability. The strong negative correlations between POLQ expression and responses to multiple chemotherapeutic agents, with molecular docking predicted potential direct interactions between vincristine, paclitaxel, docetaxel and the POLQ protein. In UCEC, high POLQ activated DNA replication, cell cycle and ATR-dependent DNA damage pathways. POLQ is a pan-cancer prognostic and therapeutic biomarker. In UCEC, it accelerates tumor progression via DNA damage and cell cycle dysregulation and reshapes immune microenvironment, supporting POLQ-targeted precision immunotherapy especially for endometrial cancer.

items.title: BEND 2.0: Benchmarking the Capabilities Needed to Design DNA
items.abstract_or_text: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits. But successful design requires capabilities that current benchmarks do not measure. Here we introduce BEND 2.0 (BENchmark for DNA language models), which tests how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether these predictions can guide sequence design. Across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets, we find that model choice and how representations are accessed both affect performance. Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or exceed models' native outputs, and functional post-training substantially improves the models' capabilities. Linear readouts transfer well across experimental assays and genes, suggesting that models capture functional patterns beyond the data used to fit individual predictors. At the same time, strong prediction of average effects can conceal weaker prediction of context-specific effects, and accurate prediction of combined mutation effects does not imply accurate prediction of their interactions. In design tasks, model predictions can reduce the number of candidates needed to find a desired response, but still leave substantial room for better design choices, particularly for context-specific and multi-cell objectives. Our benchmark reveals that genomic models now display signs of general utility but have yet to saturate on performance in even simple tasks.

items.title: Bayesian Sequential Optimal Experimental Design for Single-Pixel Imaging using Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Adaptive compressed sensing (CS) aims to select the most informative measurements sequentially, which is crucial for many modern imaging systems. This task can be formulated as a Bayesian sequential optimal experimental design (sOED) problem, where each new acquisition is chosen to maximally reduce uncertainty about the unknown image given prior information and subsequent data provided by acquisitions. However, in single-pixel imaging (SPI), the large design space consists of all possible binary illumination patterns. Directly optimizing the Bayesian sOED objective over this space using conventional methods is generally challenging. In this work, we reformulate sOED for SPI as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem. In RL, an agent learns a policy through repeated experimental trials to maximize a reward, here given as the expected information gain, the most complete measure of uncertainty reduction in Bayesian OED. This avoids the need to directly optimize complex information-theoretic objectives during a measurement to obtain the next design. Instead, the result is a learned policy function that directly maps the current posterior belief about the image to the next optimal binary measurement pattern, in a computationally efficient way. Using a simple yet representative SPI imaging scenario, this work evaluates the scalability of the learned policy under two different policy parameterizations. Furthermore, we investigate how performance deteriorates when only approximate posterior information is available or the measurements are impaired by noise, and propose several strategies to introduce additional design constraints motivated by biomedical applications. The numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed Bayesian sOED-RL framework remains robust and can be extended to more complex, large-scale SPI scenarios.

items.title: Kinetics and Evolution-guided Design of High Fidelity CRISPR-Cas Endonucleases
items.abstract_or_text: Finding high-fidelity CRISPR-Cas variants is critical for both the precision of in vitro DNA detection and the safety of in vivo gene-editing therapeutics. However, the large size of the Cas enzymes and the distinct selection criteria between its natural evolution and clinical practice lead to extensive experimental trials and limited success rate for de novo design, directed evolution and protein language model (PLM)-based filtering. Here, we present a physics-driven, PLM-assisted approach that utilizes atomistic molecular dynamics simulations and automated path searching to efficiently obtain the atom-level kinetic insights, including the transition state structures, for the conformational changes of R-loop formation that dictate the off-target DNA recognition and cleavage by Cas. We show that these kinetic insights can pinpoint the fidelity-diminishing protein residues during the early stage of target recognition. Integrated with PLM-filtering of the mutants on these sites, this approach identified high-fidelity SpyCas9 and FnCas12a variants (4.49-fold and 6.69-fold increase respectively from wild-type), surpassing previously reported counterparts at minimal cost of only a few wet-lab validations (cellular genome-editing and ribonucleoprotein cleavage assays respectively).

items.title: SPaRTA: Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Spatial-omics technologies provide clinicians, pathologists, and biomedical researchers with high-resolution maps of transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic activity within tissues. However, querying these complex datasets often requires specialized computational expertise, limiting their accessibility to domain experts without programming experience. In the current manuscript, we develop SPaRTA (Spatial Reasoning in Text-to-SQL for Omics Analysis), a natural-language interface that translates free-text questions into executable spatial SQL queries over such data. We release SPaRTA-Bench, comprising dataset-specific database schemas, explicit query conventions, and 7,500 question-SQL pairs validated through LLM-assisted verification and targeted human review, spanning breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, and melanoma tissue sections, and identify 15 failure modes in which a query runs but returns a wrong answer. Open-weight large language models (LLMs) of the Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and Phi families reach 10-40% execution accuracy zero-shot, and at most 61% with reasoning and execution feedback. Fine-tuning raises them to 63-77%, and they lose at most 6 percentage points on a tissue unseen in training. Execution feedback repairs queries that fail to run, but rarely queries that run and return a wrong answer.

items.title: CryoID2: deep learning-enhanced identification of protein and RNA from cryoEM maps
items.abstract_or_text: Identifying the molecular components of cryoEM/cryoET maps of endogenous or poorly characterized complexes remains a major bottleneck. CryoID2 addresses this by integrating deep learning-based feature prediction with sequence prioritization and structural evaluation. Three 3D U-Nets extract structure classes, key-atom positions, and reduced residue/nucleotide types from the input map. These predictions support backbone tracing and the generation of short sequence queries that rank candidates from a user-supplied pool-using BLASTp for proteins and a maximin strategy for RNA. Corresponding PDB or AlphaFold models are then retrieved, rigidly fitted using predicted features and experimental density, and ranked by map agreement. Module-level tests show high-recall feature prediction and resolution-dependent atom clustering, while a 52-case benchmark recovers near-reference fitting quality. In practice, cryoID2 correctly identified PfA-M17 from a 166-protein mass-spectrometry pool and the unannotated Ca-raiA RNA from a genome-derived non-coding sequence set, demonstrating a unified sequence-plus-structure route to molecular identification in cryoEM maps.

items.title: MedPhysBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Language Models on Medical Physics Calculations and Error Detection
items.abstract_or_text: Medical physicists turn a prescription into a delivered dose and check one another's calculations, because one error in a beam calibration or a monitor-unit (MU) calculation can affect every patient treated with it. MedPhysBench has ten seeded generators of calculation items in radiation therapy, diagnostic imaging, nuclear medicine and radiation protection, up to clinical tasks such as a TG-51 calibration worksheet. Reference answers come from code implementing the governing protocols, and a grader converts units and applies tolerance bands. From the same inputs, separate checking items test error detection, showing a colleague's worksheet or only the colleague's result, half correct and half with one planted error. On a held-out test split of 1,200 items (half for two models), 12 models scored 33.3 to 100.0% on calculation. Of the nine answers graded incorrect for the four best (99.3-100.0%), five contained model errors and four followed NCRP Report 151 on points our items misstate or leave open. Below them, most models did worst on level-3 clinical tasks, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 omitted the inverse-square correction in 19 of 20 isocentric MU items. Five models detected at least 96.7% of mostly large planted errors with at most 4% false alarms; for four of the other seven, checking only the result raised false alarms significantly. In an exploratory targeted test with 20 public cases of an omitted inverse-square correction, the three best models tested caught it in every worksheet, and three weaker models accepted 16 to 18 of 20 planted worksheets, one of them while applying the correction in most of its own calculations. Claude Opus 5.5 accepted 6 of 20 wrong results, although it applied the correction in all 20 of its own. We report the effect of two problems in our shielding items, found after the runs, and release the code, per-item outcomes and targeted-test responses.

items.title: Agentic Discovery Transfer Enables Cross-Cancer Discovery at Scale
items.abstract_or_text: Cancer research generates tens of thousands of studies each year, yet whether a published finding holds in another cancer type or patient population is rarely tested as doing so is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We define this task as discovery transfer and present SMART, a multi-agent large language model framework for discovery transfer in single-cell RNA-sequencing studies. Given a source manuscript and a target dataset, SMART extracts major clinical and mechanistic findings, generates and executes analyses for the testable findings, reports which findings transfer, and suggests follow-up. Applied to 121 studies across six cancer types, SMART identified findings that transfer across cancers, including a lung cancer prognostic signature that we confirmed to be associated with survival in liver cancer, pancreatic cancer and pleural mesothelioma. SMART also generated new mechanistic hypotheses, demonstrating how agentic discovery transfer can extend published findings beyond their original setting.

items.title: VIGAT: VLM-guided gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq
items.abstract_or_text: Summary: Gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq is challenging because genomic regions informative of cell identity can vary across genes and tissues, while broadly accessible regions may provide limited cell-type-discriminative information. We developed VIGAT, a vision-language model (VLM)-guided tool that automates visual interpretation of ATAC coverage plots for adaptive gene activity quantification. VIGAT jointly examines accessibility patterns across multiple marker genes, integrating genomic annotations and biological context to select gene-specific regions enriched for cluster-discriminative signals. Selected regions are used to generate a gene-by-cell activity matrix. Across 196 paired single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq datasets, VIGAT outperformed five existing methods in recovering marker-associated accessibility enriched in the corresponding cell populations, demonstrating the utility of VLM-guided visual reasoning for scalable gene activity quantification. Availability and implementation: VIGAT is implemented as an open-source R package and is freely available at https://github.com/beijie02/VIGAT.

items.title: Addressing the Cognitive Care Gap in Parkinson's Disease through Participatory Co-design of a Digital Neuropsychological Assessment Platform
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Cognitive impairment is a prevalent and clinically significant feature of Parkinson’s disease (PD), although systematic neuropsychological assessment remains inconsistently integrated into movement disorder clinical care. Time constraints, limited neuropsychology workforce capacity, and fragmented data infrastructure impede early identification and longitudinal monitoring of cognitive decline in this population. The ‘PDCogniCare’ program aimed to address this gap by developing best-practice guidelines and a PD-specific neuropsychological toolkit. To implement this program in clinical settings, the PDCogniCare digital platform was co-designed and developed as a web-based tool to improve access to cognitive assessment, support clinician training, competence and confidence, and enable longitudinal tracking of neuropsychological outcomes across Movement disorders and psychology services. A participatory asynchronous co-design methodology was employed across three workshops and an interim system evaluation, across metropolitan health services in Queensland, Australia. Fifteen participants were involved, encompassing all interest holders in the neuropsychological assessment journey. Design activities included journey map refinement, MoSCoW feature prioritisation, low-fidelity prototype development, and iterative platform evaluation. Consumer and caregiver input was integrated throughout. The finalised platform received a mean System Usability Scale score of 82.5, placing it in the excellent range. Participants confirmed broad alignment between the platform and their clinical and lived experience priorities. Remaining concerns, including system integration, client enrolment, clinical pathway gaps, and data governance issues, were identified as priorities for future refinement prior to wider implementation. The findings support participatory co-design as an effective methodology for developing acceptable and clinically grounded digital health tools in neurodegenerative disease contexts.

items.title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control
items.abstract_or_text: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control.

items.title: RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs
items.abstract_or_text: Reinforcement learning (RL) has improved the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks. However, token-level RL assigns an action's advantage to the entire generated response, including tokens specifying the parsed action, reasoning chains, and malformed content. Although the environment executes only the parsed action, variation in how the action is expressed in natural language can introduce additional variance into policy-gradient estimates. We propose RLiD (Reinforcement Learning in the Decision plane), a framework that directly optimizes the probabilities of executable action options. RLiD compiles observations, an optional compact memory, and a labeled action menu into the model input, and uses a large decision model (LDM) to select an action in a single forward pass. By eliminating autoregressive token generation and bypassing action parsing, RLiD avoids invalid action outputs and improves RL rollout efficiency. Our analysis shows that, within a fixed text policy, marginalizing over alternative realizations of the same action removes a zero-mean gradient component without changing the expected update. We further distill trained LDM policies into generative LLMs through supervision on their action trajectories. Experiments on ARC, Countdown, and Sokoban demonstrate improved performance or lower computational cost across several settings. On ALFWorld, the complete training and distillation pipeline reaches 99.3% success in 12.7 H100 GPU-hours, compared with 86.6% in 17.3 GPU-hours for token-level RL of the same LLM. With compiled memory, our strongest Qwen2.5-1.5B LDM and distilled generative LLM achieve 100% success on all 134 unseen and 140 seen ALFWorld evaluation games.

items.title: HNRNPC-mediated RNA processing promotes VHL-associated excessive vasculogenesis in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome revealed from patient-derived blood vessel models
items.abstract_or_text: Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome (VHLS) is an inherited disorder characterized by excessive vascularization, which contributes to the development of hemangioblastomas and benign or malignant tumors, as well as renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and cysts in multiple organs. VHLS is caused by mutations in VHL tumor suppressor gene, which encodes a component of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. Although therapeutic agents targeting hypoxia-inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF2A), which is stabilized by VHL loss and promotes tumor angiogenesis, have been approved for clinical use, their therapeutic response remains limited in RCC patients associated with VHLS. Therefore, there is an unmet need for the development of alternative therapeutic approaches independent of HIF2A. Here, we establish a human iPSCs-based model of VHLS-associated excessive vasculogenesis using induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from VHLS patients and VHL-edited isogenic iPSC lines. Vascular cells (VCs) differentiated from these VHLS-specific iPSCs exhibited excessive blood vessel formation compared to healthy donor-derived VCs, leading to vascular lesion formation characterized by abundant blood vessels and abnormal cellular growth in vivo. Mechanistically, RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) were preferentially stabilized in the patient-VCs. Among these RBPs, the stabilization of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C1/C2 (HNRNPC), which is a substrate for pVHL-mediated protein degradation independent of HIF2A expression, was critical for the dysregulated vascularization caused by VHL inactivation in this model. These findings provide an iPSCs-derived vascular platform to elucidate VHLS mechanisms and identify HNRNPC as a potential therapeutic target for VHL-driven vascular lesion formations through an HIF2A-independent mechanism.

items.title: Prediction of early Toxoplasma gondii infection during pregnancy combining host biomarkers and machine learning
items.abstract_or_text: Toxoplasma gondii is a major cause of reproductive failure and severe gestational complications in both humans and small ruminants and early diagnosis is essential to prevent adverse outcomes. In sheep, congenital toxoplasmosis can trigger early fetal death (EFD) during the acute phase of the infection (days 7-14 post-infection) when conventional diagnosis methods are ineffective. Therefore, this study aimed to identify early infection biomarkers using a machine learning approach to support EFD diagnosis and providing a translational foundation for early diagnostic strategies in human toxoplasmosis. For that, 27 serum biomarkers (cytokines, acute-phase proteins, oxidative stress and hemostatic parameters) were evaluated during the early stage of infection in 22 pregnant sheep experimentally challenged with T. gondii and 6 uninfected controls. To assess diagnostic specificity, models were tested using sera from animals experimentally infected with other abortifacient agents (Neospora caninum and Chlamydia abortus) and validated with samples from 19 natural abortion outbreaks. A four-biomarkers panel, encompassing CXCL9, CXCL10, IFN-{gamma}, and serum amyloid A, achieved over 74% accuracy in the specific detection of early T. gondii infection and 100% of sensitivity when studying natural infection cases. This approach might support the development of rapid diagnostic strategies, improving early intervention and disease management in livestock production systems. Its translation to human medicine could also aid in addressing current diagnostic gaps and facilitate timely interventions to prevent congenital toxoplasmosis and pregnancy loss in women.

items.title: Comparative molecular analysis of histopathologic subtypes reveals shared epithelial remodeling yet distinct fibroblast programs in scleroderma lung disease
items.abstract_or_text: Rationale: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) drives mortality in systemic sclerosis (SSc), with a subset developing progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) resembling idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Despite recognition of two distinct histopathologic patterns, the cellular basis of nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) and usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) remains poorly understood. Objectives: To define shared and distinct cellular and molecular features of SSc-NSIP and SSc-UIP compared to IPF. Methods: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were performed on explanted lungs from patients with SSc-NSIP (n=6), SSc-UIP (n=6), or IPF (n=6), and control donors (n=12) with immunohistochemistry and western blot validation. Main Results: Across 120,254 nuclei from 35 cell types, there was striking similarity across fibrotic subgroups in epithelial, endothelial, and immune compartments, including alveolar type 1 cell loss, pathologic alveolar type 2 (AT2) gene expression, and expansion of COL15A1 endothelial cells and profibrotic macrophages. Diseased AT2s showed activation of the p53/DNA damage pathway. Aberrant basaloid (AB) cells were present in both SSc-ILD subtypes and transcriptionally similar to IPF ABs. They consistently neighbored profibrotic CTHRC1 fibroblasts, even in SSc-NSIP, despite lacking fibroblast foci. Fibroblast heterogeneity differentiated the histopathologic subtypes. Inflammatory fibroblasts were enriched in SSc-NSIP and CTHRC1 fibroblasts in UIP. AB-to-pathologic fibroblast crosstalk was defined by profibrotic signaling, with amplified TGF-{beta} signaling in UIP. Conclusions: Convergent epithelial remodeling is a hallmark of PPF in SSc-ILD and IPF. Fibroblast heterogeneity characterized by altered TGF-beta signaling distinguishes SSc-NSIP from SSc-UIP and IPF. Accelerated aging, DNA damage, and p53-dependent senescence pathways may represent shared drivers of PPF.

items.title: RAPTORGraph: graph-based pathway modeling for causal discovery in single-cell perturbations
items.abstract_or_text: Experiments involving the perturbation of individual cells are central to understanding cellular mechanisms and can accelerate drug discovery. Causal representation learning allows us to uncover the latent factors that regulate biological systems and predict the impact of novel perturbations. Unfortunately, existing methods fail to address intervention spillover in a closed-world setting where intervention targets are known a priori, such as in Perturb-seq experiments, due to their reliance on dense encoders. Furthermore, incorporating curated biological pathways into the model imposes a confirmatory bias, forcing it to explain the data through preexisting pathways and reducing the set of hypotheses the model can explore, while discarding novel signals that lie outside the annotated pathways. In this work, we introduce RAPTORGraph, a {beta}-variational autoencoder with a GraphPathway encoder that explicitly models complex gene-to-gene interactions within learned pathways. Moreover, our model's preconditioning isolates the influence of perturbed genes, yielding clean, single-node latent interventions required for identifiable causal discovery and eliminating spillover.
